# Worksheet: Describing Your Data

[📥 Download the data (.csv)](data/pine_data.csv){.btn .btn-primary download="pine_data.csv"} [📥 Download the data (.xlsx)](data/pine_data.xlsx){.btn .btn-primary download="pine_data.xlsx"}

> ## How to use this worksheet
>
> Work through each part in order, at your own pace. Type every line of code yourself into a **plain R script** — do not copy-paste. Blocks marked **▶ Run this** are code you should type and execute. Blocks marked **✏️ Your turn** ask you to write, modify, or answer something. Boxes marked **🚀 If you finish early** are optional bonus material.
>
> **Every grey `r` box below is code you type into an R script — not into the Console.** Before you start: **File → New File → R Script**, and save it as `03_descriptive_stats.R` in your project's `scripts/` folder. Then work down the worksheet, adding each block to the bottom of that one script, in order.
>
> **Type the `# ── Part …` header comment at the top of each block, too.** Those comment lines are not decoration — they are how your script stays navigable, how you find your way back to a block that broke, and how I find your work when I read your script. A block with no header comment is a block I cannot place. In RStudio they also show up in the document outline (the `≡` button at the bottom-left of the editor) so you can jump straight to any part.

::: callout-important
## Column names in `pine_data.csv` / `pine_data.xlsx`

Both files hold the **same six columns, with exactly these names**. Type them
exactly as written — R is case-sensitive, and `Needle_Length` or `needle_length`
will not work:

| Column             | What it is                                     |
|--------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `source_file`      | the raw team file the row came from             |
| `team`             | field team — one team = **one tree**            |
| `replicate`        | needle number within a tree side (1-8)          |
| `side`             | sun exposure — `"shady"` or `"sunny"`           |
| `needle_length_mm` | needle length, millimetres                      |
| `needle_width_mm`  | needle width, millimetres                       |

After you read the file in, run `names(pine_df)` and check the names on your
screen against this table before you write any other code.
:::

# Part 1 · Load and split the data

**▶ Run this in your Script:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.1 · Load and split the data ──────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)

pine_df <- read_csv("data/pine_data.csv")

shady_df <- pine_df |> filter(side == "shady")
sunny_df <- pine_df |> filter(side == "sunny")

shady_df
```

`filter()` picks **rows** and hands back a data frame — same six columns, fewer
rows. Everything from here on stays a data frame, summarized with the pipe.

# Part 2 · Mean and median

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 3 (Describing Data) and Gotelli & Ellison Ch. 3 (Summary Statistics) on Canvas.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 2.1 · Mean and median ──────────────────────────────────────────
shady_df |>
  summarize(mean_mm = mean(needle_length_mm),
            med_mm  = median(needle_length_mm))

sunny_df |>
  summarize(mean_mm = mean(needle_length_mm),
            med_mm  = median(needle_length_mm))
```

# Part 3 · Variance and standard deviation

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 3 on variance and standard deviation; Gotelli & Ellison Ch. 3 on measures of spread.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 3.1 · Variance and standard deviation ──────────────────────────
shady_df |>
  summarize(var_mm = var(needle_length_mm),
            sd_mm  = sd(needle_length_mm))

sunny_df |>
  summarize(var_mm = var(needle_length_mm),
            sd_mm  = sd(needle_length_mm))
```

# Part 3b · Quantiles, range, and IQR

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2 (Displaying Data) — the box in a boxplot *is* the IQR.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 3b.1 · Quantiles, range, and IQR ───────────────────────────────
shady_df |>
  summarize(
    min_mm   = min(needle_length_mm),
    q25_mm   = quantile(needle_length_mm, 0.25),
    med_mm   = median(needle_length_mm),
    q75_mm   = quantile(needle_length_mm, 0.75),
    max_mm   = max(needle_length_mm),
    range_mm = max_mm - min_mm,
    iqr_mm   = IQR(needle_length_mm)
  )
```

# Part 4 · The `length()` trap

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §18 — Missing values](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/missing-values.html).

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4.1 · The `length()` trap ──────────────────────────────────────
na_demo_df <- tibble(length_mm = c(4, 3, NA, 7, NA))

na_demo_df |>
  summarize(
    rows        = n(),                     # every row, missing values included
    missing     = sum(is.na(length_mm)),
    real_values = sum(!is.na(length_mm))   # the n you actually want
  )
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Explain in your own words why `n()` gives the wrong answer for a sample size when there are missing values.

```         



________________________________________________________
```

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4.2 · The `length()` trap ──────────────────────────────────────
na_demo_df |>
  summarize(
    wrong_n  = n(),
    right_n  = sum(!is.na(length_mm)),
    sd_mm    = sd(length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    wrong_se = sd_mm / sqrt(wrong_n),
    right_se = sd_mm / sqrt(right_n)
  )
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Are `wrong_se` and `right_se` the same number? Why or why not?

`________________________`

::: callout-tip
**🚀 If you finish early:** Add a third `NA` to `length_mm` when you build `na_demo_df`, then rerun. What happens to `wrong_se` and `right_se` this time?
:::

# Part 5 · Standard error, on real data

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 4 (Estimating with Uncertainty) — the chapter for the standard error.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 5.1 · Standard error, on real data ─────────────────────────────
shady_df |>
  summarize(
    n     = sum(!is.na(needle_length_mm)),
    sd_mm = sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_mm = sd_mm / sqrt(n)
  )

sunny_df |>
  summarize(
    n     = sum(!is.na(needle_length_mm)),
    sd_mm = sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_mm = sd_mm / sqrt(n)
  )
```

# Part 6 · All stats, one group, one `summarize()`

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §3.5 — Groups and `summarize()`](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-transform.html#sec-summarize).

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 6.1 · All stats, one group, one `summarize()` ──────────────────
shady_df |>
  summarize(
    n       = sum(!is.na(needle_length_mm)),
    mean_mm = round(mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    med_mm  = round(median(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    sd_mm   = round(sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    se_mm   = round(sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n), 2)
  )
```

# Part 7 · Tidy group stats — `group_by()` + `summarize()`

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §3.5 — Groups](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-transform.html#sec-summarize).

You just wrote the same `summarize()` twice — once for `shady_df`, once for
`sunny_df`. `group_by()` removes that duplication: it splits the **whole**
data frame by a column, and `summarize()` then returns one row per group. No
`filter()`, no two objects to keep in step.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 7.1 · Tidy group stats ─────────────────────────────────────────
side_stats_df <- pine_df |>
  group_by(side) |>
  summarize(
    n       = sum(!is.na(needle_length_mm)),
    mean_mm = round(mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    med_mm  = round(median(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    sd_mm   = round(sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    se_mm   = round(sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n), 2)
  )

side_stats_df
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** Compute `se_mm` from the **raw** `sd()`, not from the
> `sd_mm` column above it — that one has already been rounded, and the SE would
> inherit the rounding error. Round only what you print.

✏️ **Your turn:** Do the `mean_mm` and `se_mm` values match the ones you calculated one side at a time in Parts 2 and 5?

`Y / N`

# Part 7c · The `n` you report is a choice

> 📖 **Read more:** Gotelli & Ellison Ch. 6 (Designing Successful Field Studies) on replication and pseudoreplication; Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 4 on what the standard error is an estimate *of*.

Your side summary said **n = 32 per side**. But we sampled only **4 trees** — 8 needles from each. Counting needles as independent is the **pseudoreplication** from Getting Started.

**▶ Run this — stage 1, collapse each tree to one number:**

``` r
# ── Part 7c.1 · The `n` you report is a choice ──────────────────────────
team_means_df <- pine_df |>
  group_by(team, side) |>
  summarize(team_mean_mm = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

team_means_df
```

**▶ Run this — stage 2, summarize those team means:**

``` r
# ── Part 7c.2 · The `n` you report is a choice ──────────────────────────
side_correct_df <- team_means_df |>
  group_by(side) |>
  summarize(
    n_trees = sum(!is.na(team_mean_mm)),
    mean_mm = round(mean(team_mean_mm), 2),
    se_mm   = round(sd(team_mean_mm) / sqrt(n_trees), 2)
  )

side_correct_df
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Fill in the comparison.

```         
                 naive (n = 32)      correct (n = 4)
mean, shady:     ______              ______
mean, sunny:     ______              ______
SE, shady:       ______              ______
SE, sunny:       ______              ______
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Which changed — the means, the standard errors, or both? What does that tell you about what pseudoreplication actually damages?

# Part 7b · See it — boxplot with mean ± SE

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2 (Displaying Data), and [R4DS §10 — Exploratory data analysis](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/EDA.html).

Every number you computed today has a picture. This is the figure you will
build for the rest of the term, so it is worth getting the layers straight.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 7b.1 · See it — boxplot with mean ± SE ─────────────────────────
side_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm)) +

  # layer 1 — the spread of all 64 needles
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, fill = NA, outlier.shape = NA) +

  # layer 2 — each team's mean, faded, behind the summary
  geom_point(data = team_means_df,
             aes(y = team_mean_mm, color = team),
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
             size = 3, alpha = 0.5) +

  # layer 3 — the mean and its standard error, on top
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = 0.15) +

  labs(x = "Sun exposure",
       y = "Needle length (mm)",
       color = "Field team") +
  theme_bw()

side_plot
```

`stat_summary()` computes a statistic *while plotting* — you never have to
build a summary table first. `fun = mean` draws the mean as a point;
`fun.data = mean_se` draws the mean ± 1 standard error as an error bar.

✏️ **Your turn:** The box and the error bar show different things. Which one describes the spread of individual needles, and which describes how precisely we know the mean?

```         
Box:          ________________________________________

Error bar:    ________________________________________
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Look at the four faded team means on each side. Do all four teams agree, or is one tree pulling its side around?

**▶ Run this — save it:**

``` r
# ── Part 7b.2 · See it — boxplot with mean ± SE ─────────────────────────
ggsave("figures/pine_side_mean_se.png",
       plot   = side_plot,
       width  = 5,
       height = 4,
       units  = "in",
       dpi    = 300)
```

::: callout-important
**⚠️ Those error bars are the naive ones.** `stat_summary()` used all 32
needles per side, so it drew the **n = 32** standard error — the
pseudoreplicated one from Part 7c. The honest error bar uses the **4 team
means**.

# Getting unstuck

When code breaks — and it will, that is normal:

1.  **Read the error message out loud.** R usually names the line and the problem.
2.  **Check the usual suspects:** did you run `library(tidyverse)`? Spelling? Did you forget `na.rm = TRUE`?
3.  `?function_name` opens the built-in help page.
4.  **Bring the exact error** (copy-paste it) to class or office hours.

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §8 — Workflow: getting help](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-help.html).

> 💡 **Key idea:** Every working scientist googles error messages daily. Getting stuck is not failing — it is the job.
